title: The spotlight effect exaggerates how much others notice you
summary: People are usually more focused on themselves than on your small mistakes.
lead: We often assume our appearance, awkward moment, or error is highly visible. Research finds people overestimate how much others notice them.
take: Your internal attention is not a measure of others' attention.
A minor slip usually fades quickly from other people's minds.
Use this to act despite ordinary embarrassment—not to ignore genuine feedback.
try: Do one useful thing today without waiting until you feel perfectly confident.
source: Spotlight-effect research by Thomas Gilovich and colleagues.

title: Correlation is not causation
summary: Two things moving together does not prove one caused the other.
lead: A relationship between variables can arise from coincidence, reverse causality, or a third factor influencing both.
take: Ask what else could explain the pattern.
Check whether the cause came before the effect.
Look for controlled evidence, not just a compelling story.
try: When you hear a claim that X causes Y, name one alternative explanation.

title: Make your environment do part of the work
summary: Behavior is shaped by cues and friction, not just willpower.
lead: A desired behavior becomes easier when its tools are visible and ready; an unwanted behavior becomes harder when extra steps are introduced.
take: Put cues for good habits in sight.
Add friction to distracting apps or routines.
Design for the tired version of yourself.
try: Prepare the exact materials for tomorrow's most important task before bed.

title: The cost of a purchase includes its opportunity cost
summary: Money spent cannot simultaneously serve another goal.
lead: A purchase is not only its price. It also represents the alternative use of those funds, such as a reserve, debt repayment, or investment.
take: Compare purchases with your actual priorities.
Separate recurring costs from one-time costs.
Use a pause for nonessential purchases.
try: Before one discretionary purchase, state what goal that money would otherwise support.

title: Ask one precise question at a time
summary: Specific questions produce clearer answers and reduce misunderstanding.
lead: Broad or stacked questions can make it difficult to identify what response is needed. Narrow questions improve shared understanding.
take: State the context briefly.
Ask for one missing fact or decision.
Confirm the answer before moving on.
try: Rewrite a multi-part question into its single most important question.

title: A map is not the territory
summary: Your model of reality is useful, but it is not reality itself.
lead: A description, label, or mental model leaves out details. Treating the model as complete can cause confident mistakes.
take: Distinguish observations from labels.
Update your view when new evidence arrives.
Use models for decisions, not as unquestionable truth.
try: For a belief you hold strongly, write what evidence would make you revise it.

title: Consistency beats occasional extremes
summary: A sustainable routine is easier to maintain than repeated all-or-nothing efforts.
lead: Plans that fit real schedules and recovery needs are more likely to persist than bursts of intensity followed by exhaustion.
take: Choose a manageable baseline.
Increase gradually when the baseline is stable.
Treat missed days as data, not a reason to abandon the plan.
try: Define a minimum workout or learning session that can fit even a busy day.

title: Assume ambiguity before assuming hostility
summary: A delayed reply or terse message can have many explanations.
lead: Sparse communication is ambiguous. Jumping straight to hostile intent can trigger unnecessary conflict.
take: Separate the observable event from your interpretation.
Consider benign alternatives without dismissing repeated patterns.
Clarify directly when the issue matters.
try: Before reacting to a message, write two explanations besides your first interpretation.

title: A confident answer is not proof
summary: Fluency can hide errors in people, systems, and AI outputs.
lead: Presentation quality and factual reliability are separate. Verification should depend on stakes, not on how convincing an answer sounds.
take: Check dates, figures, and quoted claims.
Prefer primary sources for important decisions.
Treat uncertainty honestly.
try: Verify the next surprising factual claim using an authoritative source.

title: Use closed-loop communication for critical instructions
summary: A message is not complete until receipt and understanding are confirmed.
lead: In operational environments, transmitting a message alone may not ensure it was heard or understood. Repeat-back and confirmation reduce ambiguity.
take: Deliver concise, unambiguous information.
Have the receiver repeat critical details where procedure requires.
Correct mismatches immediately and follow approved SOP.
try: Practice concise repeat-back wording for a routine, non-sensitive instruction.
source: Aviation human-factors concept; approved company procedures take precedence.

title: Name the emotion to create a little distance
summary: Labeling what you feel can help you respond instead of react.
lead: Putting an emotion into words can reduce its intensity for some people and make the situation easier to evaluate.
take: Use a specific label rather than 'bad'.
Notice the trigger and physical cues.
Emotion is information, not an instruction.
try: In a tense moment, silently name the feeling and identify the actual problem.
source: Affect-labeling research; effects vary by context.

title: Protect the first minutes of a task
summary: A clean start reduces the chance that setup and distractions consume the session.
lead: Starting often involves more friction than continuing. A short, preplanned opening sequence can help move from intention to action.
take: Define the first step before the session.
Keep relevant tools ready.
Delay unrelated messages until after the initial focus block.
try: Write a one-line start instruction for tomorrow's priority.

title: Diversification manages concentration risk
summary: Owning different exposures can reduce dependence on one outcome.
lead: Diversification cannot eliminate market risk or guarantee returns, but it can reduce the impact of a single holding or sector dominating a portfolio.
take: Avoid confusing many ticker symbols with true diversification.
Consider sector, asset, and geographic overlap.
Match risk to your time horizon and ability to absorb losses.
try: Check whether several investments you own are exposed to the same underlying risk.

title: The base rate is the starting point
summary: Before judging an unusual story, consider how common the event is overall.
lead: A vivid example can distort judgment. Base rates provide the background probability against which new evidence should be assessed.
take: Ask how often this happens generally.
Compare the case with relevant reference groups.
Update with evidence instead of ignoring the baseline.
try: For a claim about a rare event, find a credible estimate of its general frequency.

title: A concise summary is a test of understanding
summary: If you cannot explain the point simply, you may not yet know its structure.
lead: Summarizing forces you to distinguish central claims from supporting detail. Simplicity should preserve meaning, not erase nuance.
take: Identify the main claim.
Keep only essential supporting reasons.
Mention important limitations.
try: Summarize something you learned today in two sentences without losing its key caveat.

title: Use feedback to adjust the method, not your identity
summary: A result can reveal a strategy problem without defining your worth or ability.
lead: Treating a setback as information keeps attention on variables that can be changed: preparation, timing, practice, or approach.
take: Describe the result objectively.
Identify one controllable factor.
Change one thing and test again.
try: Turn one recent frustration into a specific adjustment for your next attempt.

title: Choose principles before pressure arrives
summary: Pre-decided rules reduce impulsive choices in difficult moments.
lead: When tired, stressed, or tempted, people may abandon long-term priorities. A few clear personal rules can serve as decision constraints.
take: Make rules specific and realistic.
Use them for recurring situations.
Review and revise them based on evidence.
try: Write one rule for handling an impulse purchase, heated reply, or missed routine.

title: Recovery is part of training
summary: Rest is not the opposite of progress; it supports adaptation.
lead: Physical improvement depends on training stimulus plus adequate recovery. More effort is not always better when fatigue accumulates.
take: Respect sleep and rest days.
Increase training load gradually.
Notice persistent pain or unusual fatigue and respond appropriately.
try: Plan recovery time into your next week's activity instead of leaving it accidental.

title: Repair small misunderstandings early
summary: A brief clarification can prevent an avoidable conflict from growing.
lead: When a conversation goes wrong, a prompt and specific repair can reset shared understanding without assigning blame.
take: State what you think was misunderstood.
Own your part where appropriate.
Ask what would clarify the issue.
try: Use: 'I think I explained that poorly. What I meant was…' when needed.

title: Automate repetition, keep judgment human
summary: Automation is strongest on predictable tasks; oversight matters for exceptions.
lead: Rules-based systems can save time on routine operations, but context, edge cases, and consequential decisions need checks.
take: Automate a stable workflow first.
Define failure conditions and review points.
Keep a human accountable for high-stakes outcomes.
try: Identify one repetitive low-risk task and write its steps clearly enough to automate.
